house.d: Early-1980s Chicago: at The Warehouse, Frankie Knuckles re-edited disco and layered it over drum machines, making music built for dancefloor loops; the name comes from that club. It inherited disco's 4/4 pulse and soulful vocals, and directly spun off the deep, acid and garage branches.

chicago-house.d: The concrete early form of house: TR-808/909 drum machines, rough sampling and soulful vocals; the labels Trax and DJ International defined its sound.

acid-house.d: Its squealing sound comes from the Roland TB-303's glide and resonance; Phuture's 1987 "Acid Tracks" gave it its name, and its arrival in the UK in 1988 ignited the Second Summer of Love.

deep-house.d: Slower, more soulful house that prizes chords, atmosphere and low end; Larry Heard's "Can You Feel It" is the template.

garage-house.d: A New York/New Jersey offshoot of house named after Larry Levan's Paradise Garage; gospel-style vocals and swingier drums, it later crossed to Britain and became UK garage.

hip-house.d: House beats plus rap: the first formal marriage of two Black dancefloor cultures.

vocal-house.d: Traditional house built around a singer, with choruses and harmonies aimed straight at the dancefloor.

progressive-house.d: Long passages, gradual builds, an emphasis on atmosphere and tension; trance-influenced, it later became the skeleton of mainstage EDM.

tech-house.d: House groove plus techno's cold, hard timbres, minimal and looping, built for long DJ sets.

funky-house.d: Filtered house sampling disco and funk that reached the mainstream around the 2000s.

microhouse.d: Minimal, clicky and sparse in the low end, stripping house down to nothing but breathing.

minimal-house.d: Mid-2000s minimal house that sustains its groove through the tiniest shifts.

electro-house.d: House with distorted synths and rock-style drops that ruled the festivals around 2010.

afro-house.d: House fused with African percussion and tribal vocals; Black Coffee and others carried it to the rest of the world.

kwaito.d: A South African street variant of house: slow tempos, spoken-word rapping, ghetto culture.

amapiano.d: A new South African sound of deep house, kwaito and gqom: piano chords and log-drum bass, a worldwide hit in the 2020s.

tropical-house.d: Light house beats plus tropical timbres; Kygo turned it into global pop.

slap-house.d: Slapped bass plus pop vocals: European dance music for the TikTok era.

future-house.d: Springy bass and chopped vocals, sitting somewhere between house and EDM.

french-house.d: Disco and funk samples plus filters gave it a French touch; Daft Punk made it a global phenomenon.

disco-house.d: Disco strings and vocals laid straight over house drums, a loop back to disco.

techno.d: Detroit, 1985: the Belleville Three welded Kraftwerk's synths, funk's groove and futurist imagination into wordless, ceaselessly propulsive machine music.

acid-techno.d: Acid house's 303 sound enters techno, harder and more psychedelic.

minimal-techno.d: Everything extraneous removed, leaving only pulse and space; it developed along Detroit and Berlin lines.

dub-techno.d: Pouring dub's delay and reverb into techno; Basic Channel set the template.

hard-techno.d: Faster, harder, more industrial techno born for big warehouse parties.

melodic-techno.d: Bringing trance's melodicism back to techno; it became big-club mainstream in the late 2010s.

electro.d: 808 drum machine plus robot voices; Afrika Bambaataa's "Planet Rock" turned Kraftwerk into street music.

freestyle.d: Electro plus Latin melodies and synths, made for New York and Miami's Latin dancefloors.

miami-bass.d: 808 bass plus fast-paced rap; 2 Live Crew turned it into a byword for controversy.

baile-funk.d: Miami bass reached Rio and became favela party music, later catching on worldwide.

uk-garage.d: American garage house reached London, picked up jungle's bass and syncopation, and became UK garage.

speed-garage.d: UK garage sped up: heavier bass and faster tempos.

2-step.d: It drops the four-on-the-floor kick, keeping only syncopated drums and vocals; the direct precursor to dubstep.

dubstep.d: 2-step rhythms plus dub bass from South London's FWD>> scene; Skrillex took it global in 2010.

grime.d: Accelerated UK garage plus hardcore rap: East London's MC culture.

bassline.d: Sheffield's descendant of speed garage, named for its jumpy basslines.
